explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says Jesus sat down to teach them. All the people had come to Him, so He had a full crowd and no empty seats to worry about. I once taught a room of cookie cutters how to press dough, and half of them fell asleep.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “All the people came to Him, and He sat down to teach them.” So Jesus sat, and He taught. A crowd that big, and nobody had to hold up a sign saying class was starting.

explanations.answer: To test Him and find a reason to accuse Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, “They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him.” So the question wasn't really a question. It was a trap with a bow on it. Sort of like asking me if I want a cookie while holding a clipboard.

explanations.answer: To learn from Him what the Law means
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because it sounds like a fair question. But the text says why they asked: “They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him.” Nobody there was taking notes to learn. They were setting up an accusation.

explanations.answer: To show the whole crowd they respect Him
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, baker. They did call Him “Teacher.” But John 8:6 says they asked to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him. Calling Him Teacher was one thing. What they were after was something else.

Right, friend. The text says Jesus “bent down and began to write on the ground with His finger.” They asked Him the big question, and He bent down. I don't know about you, but I'd have been talking a mile a minute.

Not this time, baker. John 8:6 says, “Jesus bent down and began to write on the ground with His finger.” He did it right after they asked what He says. The passage doesn't tell us what He wrote, so we leave that part alone.

explanations.answer: Whoever among them is without sin
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” One sentence, and the whole mood in that courtyard changed. I've been pressing cookies for years and I've never landed a line like that.

explanations.answer: Whoever caught her in the act
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd pick it, since they did say she was caught in the act. But that's not what Jesus says. He says, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” He didn't ask who caught her. He asked who was without sin.

explanations.answer: Whoever knows the Law the best
explanations.explanation: They were scribes and Pharisees, so knowing the Law was their whole thing. But Jesus doesn't ask about that. He says, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” The test was about sin, and not about who could quote the most.
That's right, baker. The text says they “began to go away one by one.” No shouting match and no speeches. They just started heading for the exit. Quietest crowd I've ever heard of.
You'd expect shouting, wouldn't you? But the text says, “they began to go away one by one.” They left. It went from a loud accusation to people quietly walking out.
Nice thought, baker, but that's not what happened here. John 8:9 says they “began to go away one by one.” Nobody stopped to pray. They just started leaving.
Careful, friend. The text says they went away “beginning with the older ones.” So the oldest left first, not the youngest. I'd have guessed the same as you, and I'd have been wrong too.
Right, baker. John 8:9 says they began to go away one by one, “beginning with the older ones.” So the older ones were first out the door. The youngest were not the first to go.
Yes, baker. Jesus asks her, “Woman, where are your accusers?” Then He adds, “Has no one condemned you?” The crowd that dragged her in was gone, and He pointed that out to her gently.

explanations.answer: Why she came to the temple
explanations.explanation: That's not what He asks. Jesus asks her, “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you?” He doesn't ask her why she was there. He asks about the people who brought her.

explanations.answer: Who brought her to the courts
explanations.explanation: Close, because it's about her accusers. But Jesus doesn't ask who brought her. He asks, “Woman, where are your accusers?” The text already told us who brought her, so His question is about where they went.
That's right, baker. She answers, “No one, Lord.” The ones who came to condemn her were gone, and she says so plainly. Short answer, and it says everything.

I can see why you'd think that, with a whole crowd bringing her in. But the text says only Jesus was left with her. Her answer is, “No one, Lord.” Everybody had walked out, so nobody was left to condemn her.
Good try, baker. But she doesn't say that. John 8:11 has her answer, “No one, Lord.” With the accusers gone, there was no somebody left standing there.

explanations.answer: He doesn't condemn her and she should sin no more
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “Then neither do I condemn you… Now go and sin no more.” Notice He gives her both parts, and I think that's a lot of kindness in one sentence. I wish every pep talk came with that much care.

explanations.answer: He condemns her but she may go back home
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus says, “Then neither do I condemn you.” So He doesn't condemn her at all. He also tells her, “Now go and sin no more.”

explanations.answer: She must go and offer a sacrifice for her sin
explanations.explanation: I see where you're headed, since sacrifices come up a lot in the Law. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, “Then neither do I condemn you,” and then, “Now go and sin no more.” The passage doesn't mention a sacrifice.
